Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . Proposition 43: Limits Voters' Ability to Raise Revenues For Local Government Services
Proposition 43: Limits Voters' Ability to Raise Revenues For Local Government Services
Proposition 43: Limits Voters' Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
Two-Thirds Vote Requirement for Local Special Tax Initiatives and Property Tax Initiative Prohibition Amendment
Summary
Placed on the ballot via 2025-2026 Assembly Constitutional Amendment 22 (ACA 22 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22) ), Proposition 43 proposes adding Section 4.5 to Article XII of the California Constitution. The measure increases the approval threshold for citizen-initiated local special tax measures, requiring a two-thirds (66.67%) vote to enact, extend, or raise special taxes at the local level.
F iscal Impact
There is a possibility that local government tax revenues will not go up as much in the future due to a higher vote threshold for certain taxes.
What your vote means
YES: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
NO: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters argue that Proposition 43 protects taxpayers by requiring a two-thirds voter majority for local special tax increases, closing legal loopholes that previously allowed them to pass with a simple majority.
Opponents contend that this higher voting threshold allows a minority of voters to block popular measures, making it much harder for local communities to fund essential public services like schools, roads, and emergency response. Ultimately, the measure pits stronger taxpayer protections against the ability of local communities to raise funding by majority rule.

Proposition 43 : Two-thirds vote for voter-proposed local special taxes
Published September 29, 2026 · Updated November 2, 2026
Proposition 43 would require a two-thirds vote to approve local special taxes that voters put on the ballot by petition, starting January 1, 2027. Special taxes are taxes dedicated to a specific purpose. Special taxes placed on the ballot by a city council or other local board already need two-thirds, but court decisions let voter-proposed special taxes pass with a simple majority. It would also bar local governments and voters from adopting new taxes based on property value, with exceptions already in the Constitution.
Summary by CityHallPass , not the official text or legal advice. The official text controls: California Official Voter Information Guide: Proposition 43 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/).
Results
Polls close at 8 p.m. Pacific on Nov. 3. First results appear here after that.
At a glance
Proposition 43
Vote needed for a local special tax proposed by voter petition Majority today; two-thirds for measures approved after Jan. 1, 2027, if it passes
Effect on City Measure FD (same ballot) None under the official summary: FD needs a majority
How it got here Legislative deal on June 25, 2026 that removed a broader Howard Jarvis initiative. Senate 35-1, Assembly 68-2
Money raised, Jan. 2025 to Nov. 1, 2026 For: $17.56 million (two committees). Against: $9.20 million
Largest donor For: California Business Roundtable Issues PAC, $11.64 million. Against: SEIU California State Council, $1.5 million
Latest public polls PPIC, Oct. 16-22: 42% yes, 55% no. Berkeley IGS, Oct. 19-25: 36% yes, 46% no
Each figure is sourced in the sections below. Money figures come from the committees' state campaign statements and late contribution reports (Cal-Access).
Details and source links: Polls , Money for and against , The details , Sources .
What does a yes vote on Proposition 43 mean?
Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
What does a no vote on Proposition 43 mean?
Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.
What would Proposition 43 cost?
The Legislative Analyst says local governments' tax revenue could be lower in the future than it otherwise would be, because certain taxes would be harder to pass. The actual effect is unknown and depends on future decisions by local governments and voters. The analysis gives no dollar figure.
What it means for the City of LA
Future citizen-initiative special taxes in the City of Los Angeles, such as a sales tax for one department or a transfer tax like Measure ULA, would need two-thirds of the vote instead of a majority, starting January 1, 2027. The official summary says it applies to measures approved after that date, so the City's Measure FD on this ballot is decided by majority vote. Taxes the City Council puts on the ballot are not changed: general taxes still need a majority and special taxes already need two-thirds. The Legislative Analyst does not estimate the effect on the City.
The details
Official title Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Type Legislative constitutional amendment, placed on the ballot by the Legislature (ACA 22)
Votes needed to pass Simple majority (more than 50% yes) of votes cast statewide
The question on your ballot
Limits voters’ ability to pass voter-proposed local special taxes by increasing percentage of votes needed to approve such ballot measures from a majority (over 50%) to two-thirds, beginning January 1, 2027. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that local government tax revenues will not go up as much in the future due to a higher vote threshold for certain taxes. Supporters: California Taxpayers Association; Family Business Association of California; California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce Opponents: California Professional Firefighters; California Federation of Teachers; Nurse Alliance of SEIU CA.
What would change
Today If Proposition 43 passes
Local special tax placed on the ballot by a city council, county board or district Two-thirds of voters must approve (State Constitution, Art. XIII C, Sec. 2(d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%202.&article=XIII%20C)) No change (text of Proposition 43 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf))
Local special tax placed on the ballot by voter petition A majority can approve it, under recent court decisions (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/analysis.htm)) Two-thirds of voters must approve any new, increased or extended special tax proposed by voters, beginning Jan. 1, 2027 (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/analysis.htm))
Local general tax (money can go to any purpose) A majority of voters must approve (State Constitution, Art. XIII C, Sec. 2(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%202.&article=XIII%20C)) No change. The text covers only special taxes and property taxes (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf))
New local taxes based on property value Limited by Proposition 13 and later amendments No local government, “including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power,” may impose “ad valorem taxes on real property,” except as Article XIII D, Section 3(a)(1) already allows (text, Sec. 4.5(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf))
Taxes voters approved before 2027 In effect Not affected. The Attorney General’s summary says the measure “Applies to voter-proposed ballot measures approved after January 1, 2027” (official title and summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/title-summary.htm))
Proposition 43 adds one section, Section 4.5, to Article XIII A of the State Constitution, the article created by Proposition 13 in 1978 (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf)). “Local government” and “special tax” keep their existing constitutional meanings. The Legislative Analyst’s analysis does not discuss the property-tax part, subdivision (b) (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/analysis.htm)). The Sacramento Bee described it as generally barring new taxes based on property values, “with exceptions for certain voter-approved taxes used to repay bonds” (Sacramento Bee via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/should-local-taxes-require-two-thirds-voter-approval-proposition-43-explained/ar-AA2crlnQ)).
What it means for the City of Los Angeles
Measure FD on this ballot. The City’s Initiative Ordinance FD, a half-cent sales tax for the Fire Department, is a special tax placed on the Nov. 3 ballot by voter petition. The City’s impartial summary says FD takes effect if a majority approves it (City pamphlet (https://cityclerk.lacity.org/election/ENG201_NOV-2026_Voter_Info_Pamphlet.pdf#page=91)). Proposition 43 “Applies to voter-proposed ballot measures approved after January 1, 2027,” the Attorney General’s summary says (official title and summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/title-summary.htm)). Elena Q. Gerli of the law firm Burke, Williams & Sorensen wrote that “local tax measures on the November 2026 ballot are still governed by the current majority-vote rule” (California City News (https://www.californiacitynews.org/2026/08/burke-public-law-update-tax-measure-amending-california-constitution-november-ballot.html)). The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association’s argument against FD says FD “would squeeze through the loophole” before Proposition 43 takes effect in January 2027 (City pamphlet, argument against FD (https://cityclerk.lacity.org/election/ENG201_NOV-2026_Voter_Info_Pamphlet.pdf#page=97)). We found no official analysis that says otherwise. See our Measure FD page (https://cityhallpass.com/election-2026/measures/measure-fd).
Measure ULA. City voters approved Measure ULA, a citizen initiative that taxes property sales over $5 million at 4% and sales of $10 million or more at 5.5%, with 57.77% of the vote in November 2022 (County election results (https://results.lavote.gov/text-results/4300)). That share is below two-thirds. Proposition 43 does not undo taxes already approved (Burke, Williams & Sorensen (https://www.californiacitynews.org/2026/08/burke-public-law-update-tax-measure-amending-california-constitution-november-ballot.html)). The Howard Jarvis initiative that Proposition 43 replaced would have eliminated ULA and similar taxes, LAist reported (LAist, June 26, 2026 (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-mansion-tax-measure-ula-transfer-state-sacramento-ab-736-howard-jarvis-novemeber-ballot-measure)). ULA has raised $1.2 billion since April 2023, LAist reported (LAist (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-mansion-tax-measure-ula-transfer-state-sacramento-ab-736-howard-jarvis-novemeber-ballot-measure)). The Legislative Analyst says that, beginning Jan. 1, 2027, “any new, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters would require a two-thirds vote” (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/analysis.htm)). The City’s Proposition TE on this ballot, placed by the Council, would exempt some Palisades Fire victims from ULA (our Proposition TE page (https://cityhallpass.com/election-2026/measures/measure-te)).
Future City petitions. The City Clerk’s petition list shows citizen tax initiatives cleared to circulate into late 2027, including two gross receipts taxes tied to the ratio of executive to worker pay (petitions expiring Nov. 12 and Dec. 8, 2027). A half-cent sales tax for Recreation and Parks received a title in December 2025 but is not shown as approved for circulation (City Clerk petition status (https://clerk.lacity.gov/elections/petition-and-measure-info/petition-status)). The list does not say whether each tax would be general or special. Only special taxes would face the new two-thirds rule (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf)).
Council-placed taxes. Proposition 43 does not change the vote needed for taxes the City Council places on the ballot. General taxes still need a majority and special taxes still need two-thirds (State Constitution, Art. XIII C, Sec. 2 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%202.&article=XIII%20C); Aleshire & Wynder (https://www.awattorneys.com/client-updates/proposition-43-aca-22-could-reshape-local-tax-initiatives-what-california-cities-should-know-before-2027/)).
We found no official position on Proposition 43 from the Mayor, the City Council or the LA County Board of Supervisors as of Sept. 30, 2026.
How it got on the ballot
Proposition 43 began as Assembly Constitutional Amendment 22 by Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-Oakland). The resolution says it was proposed with “two-thirds of the membership of each house concurring” (text as quoted by Burke, Williams & Sorensen (https://www.californiacitynews.org/2026/08/burke-public-law-update-tax-measure-amending-california-constitution-november-ballot.html)).
2017: In California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland , the State Supreme Court ruled that a tax measure placed on the ballot by citizen initiative needs only a majority, according to Burke, Williams & Sorensen (California City News (https://www.californiacitynews.org/2026/08/burke-public-law-update-tax-measure-amending-california-constitution-november-ballot.html)). The Legislative Analyst says “recent court decisions” allow majority approval of voter-proposed special taxes (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/analysis.htm)).
Nov. 8, 2022: City of LA voters approved Measure ULA with 57.77% (County election results (https://results.lavote.gov/text-results/4300)).
Late 2025 to early 2026: The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association collected signatures for Initiative 1983, the “Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13.” Burke says it would have raised the vote for voter-initiated tax measures to two-thirds, capped local real estate transfer taxes at the state base rate, and voided noncompliant property-related taxes by the end of 2028 (California City News (https://www.californiacitynews.org/2026/08/burke-public-law-update-tax-measure-amending-california-constitution-november-ballot.html)). Its committee, then named “Californians to Restore Local Taxpayers’ Right to Vote on Taxes,” paid National Political Consultants $12.8 million for petition circulation (Cal-Access, committee 1484860 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1484860)). Real estate developers and investors paid for the initiative, LAist reported (LAist (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-mansion-tax-measure-ula-transfer-state-sacramento-ab-736-howard-jarvis-novemeber-ballot-measure)).
ACA 13: The Legislature had placed ACA 13 (Ward) on the ballot. It would have required a measure that raises a vote threshold to pass by that same higher threshold, which Burke says would have meant the Jarvis initiative needed two-thirds (California City News (https://www.californiacitynews.org/2026/08/burke-public-law-update-tax-measure-amending-california-constitution-november-ballot.html)).
June 25, 2026: Just before the deadline to remove measures from the ballot, the initiative’s proponents, Governor Gavin Newsom and legislative leaders announced a deal. Initiative 1983 and ACA 13 were withdrawn and replaced by ACA 22. The Secretary of State records that ACA 13 was removed from the ballot that day under ACA 21, Resolution Chapter 131 (Secretary of State, qualified measures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/qualified-ballot-measures); Burke, Williams & Sorensen (https://www.californiacitynews.org/2026/08/burke-public-law-update-tax-measure-amending-california-constitution-november-ballot.html); LAist (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-mansion-tax-measure-ula-transfer-state-sacramento-ab-736-howard-jarvis-novemeber-ballot-measure)). ACA 22 was introduced and passed that day: 68-2 in the Assembly and 35-1 in the Senate. Assemblymembers Alex Lee and Nick Schultz and Senator Scott Wiener voted no. It was filed with the Secretary of State as Resolution Chapter 132 at 4:40 p.m. (ACA 22 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22); ACA 22 history (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22)).
July 1, 2026: The City Council voted 14-0 to shelve a City measure that would have exempted new apartment buildings from ULA for 10 years, and 13-1 to place a Palisades Fire exemption on the ballot, now Proposition TE (LAist, July 1, 2026 (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-council-mansion-tax-measure-ula-november-ballot-measure-2026-vote)).
Jon Coupal, president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, called the deal “a tremendous turnaround” (LAist (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-mansion-tax-measure-ula-transfer-state-sacramento-ab-736-howard-jarvis-novemeber-ballot-measure)). Wicks said getting the Jarvis measure off the ballot protected local revenue from ULA and other transfer taxes (LAist (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-mansion-tax-measure-ula-transfer-state-sacramento-ab-736-howard-jarvis-novemeber-ballot-measure)). She now opposes Proposition 43. “I authored ACA 22 not because I wanted it to become law,” she posted, saying it was the only way to get the other initiative off the ballot in time, the LA Times reported (LA Times, July 6, 2026 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-06/2026-california-propositions-voter-guide-billionaires-tax-voter-id-homebuyers-money-tax-hike-limits)). The Orange County Register’s editorial board also noted that Democratic lawmakers who placed it on the ballot are asking voters to reject it (Orange County Register (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/08/09/endorsement-yes-on-proposition-43-to-make-it-harder-to-raise-taxes/)).
What each side says
In the state voter guide. Arguments are the opinions of their authors and are not checked for accuracy by any official agency (arguments and rebuttals (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).

Court decisions created “loopholes” in Proposition 13, and the measure “restores the two-thirds vote requirement to pass local special taxes.”
Local governments “have imposed over 2,000 new or higher taxes in the past decade.”

It “requires governments to spend tax revenue for the specific purpose voters approved” and “guarantees voters the right to vote on all local taxes.”
The opponents’ rebuttal says the measure “doesn’t cut your taxes a penny” and lets “just 33.4% of voters veto what nearly 67% want.” It was signed by Nick Lapis (Californians Against Waste), Bill Barnes (Non-Profit Housing Association of Northern California) and Steve Frisch (Sierra Business Council) (rebuttal (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Argument against, signed by Darrell Roberts (California Professional Firefighters), Chris Harkins (Nurse Alliance of SEIU California) and Adam Weinberger (California School Employees Association) (argument against (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/arguments-rebuttals.htm)):
It lets “just one-third of voters (33.4%) block local voter decisions.”
It “makes it harder to fund fire and police services,” roads, schools and health care.

Prop 43: Special Tax Measure limits
Proposition 43 would make it harder to create or raise certain local taxes. It would raise the share of votes needed to pass local special tax measures proposed by citizens from a simple majority to two-thirds. The measure grew out of a deal between state lawmakers and the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to keep a more restrictive tax proposal off the ballot.
Proposition 43 would make it harder to create or raise certain local taxes. It would raise the share of votes needed to pass local special tax measures proposed by citizens from a simple majority to two-thirds. The measure grew out of a deal between state lawmakers and the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to keep a more restrictive tax proposal off the ballot.
What’s at stake
A two-thirds vote is already required for special taxes proposed by local governments, but not for those proposed by individual citizens. Prop. 43 would close that gap and apply the higher bar to citizen-led initiatives as well. That could affect how communities pay for local services through voter-approved taxes.
Official title on the ballot: Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Language you will see (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/index.htm) :
Limits voters’ ability to pass voter-proposed local special taxes by increasing the percentage of votes needed to approve such ballot measures from a majority (over 50%) to two-thirds, beginning January 1, 2027.
What your vote means
A “yes” vote means: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
A “no” vote means: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.
Understanding Prop. 43
Special taxes are ones levied for a specific purpose, such as affordable housing or public transportation, while general taxes go into a city’s general fund and can be used for any city program or service. General taxes only require a simple majority to pass, regardless of who places them on the ballot.
But special taxes placed on the ballot by a local government must meet the two-thirds approval threshold. For a long time, it was assumed (https://calmatters.org/economy/2017/08/california-taxes-two-step/) that special taxes from citizen-led initiatives had to meet this higher mark. That changed in 2017 (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/), and now these initiatives only need to win over 50% of the vote.
Since then, municipalities have passed over two dozen of these initiatives with support below the two-thirds mark, according to previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/). In Los Angeles, the most high-profile recent example is Measure ULA (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-mansion-tax-measure-ula-transfer-state-sacramento-ab-736-howard-jarvis-novemeber-ballot-measure), also known as the “mansion tax,” (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-council-mansion-tax-measure-ula-november-ballot-measure-2026-vote) which passed in 2022 with 57.77% of the vote (https://results.lavote.gov/#year=2022&election=4300).
Watch the ballot cram session analysis
What supporters say
Anti-tax advocates have pushed for similar policies for years. They argue that special interest groups have taken advantage of the simple-majority threshold to pass special taxes in low-turnout elections.
Notable supporters: Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, Reform California and the Southern California News Group editorial board
What opponents say
Opponents argue the measure would limit communities’ ability to raise needed money for local services. They also say it would make it easier for wealthy interests to block tax measures that most voters support.
Notable opponents: California Democratic Party, SEIU Local 1000 and The Sacramento Bee editorial board
Fiscal impact
Because Prop. 43 would make it more difficult to pass certain taxes, local governments’ tax revenues “could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be,” according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=43&year=2026), which says the precise impact would “depend on future decisions by local governments and voters.”

Proposition 43
Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Analysis of Measure
Background
Local Governments in California. California has many local governments. These include cities, counties, special districts, and school districts.
Vote Thresholds for Local Taxes. The State Constitution allows local governments to increase taxes with local voter approval. Tax increases can be put on a ballot by voters or a local governing board (such as a city council or board of supervisors). Increases in some types of local taxes require a two-thirds vote to approve them, while other types of taxes require a majority (more than half) vote to approve them. Some local tax increases are approved permanently, while others are approved for a limited period of time. Before those taxes expire, voters can be asked whether to extend them.
Proposal
Requires Certain Local Taxes Receive Two-Thirds Approval by Voters. Under current law, local taxes that are used for a specific purpose require a two-thirds vote to be approved. These are called special taxes. However, recent court decisions have allowed special taxes that are proposed by voters to be approved with a majority vote. Under Proposition 43, beginning on January 1, 2027, any new, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters would require a two-thirds vote.
Fiscal Effects
Possibility for Lower Local Government Tax Revenues in the Future. Proposition 43 makes it harder for local governments to pass certain taxes. As a result, local governments' tax revenues could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be. The actual revenue impact is unknown and would depend on future decisions by local governments and voters.
Yes/No Statement
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
A NO vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.
Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact
Possibility that local government tax revenues will not go up as much in the future due to a higher vote threshold for certain taxes.
Ballot Label

What's on California's ballot in the 2026 midterm election? A voter's guide to the statewide races
By
Richard Ramos
Richard Ramos
Web Producer, CBS Sacramento (https://www.cbsnews.com/team/richard-ramos/)
Richard Ramos is a web producer for CBS Sacramento who was born and raised in Sacramento. He graduated with a BA in Journalism from CSUS.
Read Full Bio (https://www.cbsnews.com/team/richard-ramos/)
Richard Ramos (https://www.cbsnews.com/team/richard-ramos/)
November 2, 2026 / 6:49 AM PST
/ CBS Sacramento
Add CBS News on Google (https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=cbsnews.com)
California voters will decide the state's next governor, choose candidates for several other statewide offices and weigh in on 14 propositions when they head to the polls on Tuesday.
The ballot includes proposals on wealth taxes, affordable housing, state budget reserves, election rules, homeownership, medical research and environmental regulations.
Here's what you need to know about the statewide races on the California ballot.
Governor
Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton are competing to succeed Gov. Gavin Newsom, who is barred by term limits from seeking another term.
Becerra, a former California attorney general, served as U.S. secretary of Health and Human Services under the Biden administration. He also represented a Los Angeles-area congressional district for 24 years. Becerra's most notable endorsements include Newsom and former Vice President Kamala Harris.
Hilton is a former Fox News host who served as an adviser to former British Prime Minister David Cameron. Hilton has been formally endorsed in the race by President Trump.
Both candidates have centered their campaigns on affordability, though each has introduced vastly different proposals to address rising costs for residents.
Becerra and Hilton have differed in their approaches to lowering the state's gas prices, California's environmental policies, homelessness, healthcare and collaborating with the federal government on immigration.
Lieutenant governor
Democrat Fiona Ma and Republican Gloria Romero are running for lieutenant governor.
The lieutenant governor is first in the line of succession to the governor and serves in several state government roles, including as president of the state Senate, casting tie-breaking votes when necessary. The officeholder also serves on boards overseeing higher education.
Attorney general
California Attorney General Rob Bonta is facing Republican Michael Gates in Tuesday's election for the state's top law enforcement post.
Bonta, a Democrat, is seeking a second full term. Gates, a former Huntington Beach city attorney, has campaigned on public safety, including full enforcement of Proposition 36.
Bonta has been a leading figure in California's legal battles against the Trump administration (https://www.cbsnews.com/sacramento/news/california-rob-bonta-discusses-trump-first-100-days/) . His reelection campaign (https://robbonta.com/issues/) also emphasizes gun violence prevention, consumer protections and reproductive rights.
Gates served as Huntington Beach's elected city attorney for a decade and in 2025 worked in the Trump administration for the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division. His campaign calls for (https://www.gates4ag.com/issues) stronger prosecution of repeat offenders, increased support for law enforcement and greater local control over housing decisions.
Secretary of State
Incumbent Democrat Shirley N. Weber and Republican Donald P. Wagner are competing in the race for secretary of state.
The secretary of state is California's chief elections officer, responsible for overseeing statewide elections, maintaining election-related records and administering campaign finance and lobbying disclosure requirements. The office also handles business filings and other official state records.
Weber's campaign has emphasized strengthening election security, protecting voting rights and maintaining access to voting. Wagner's campaign has also focused on election security, offering his support of Proposition 39, which aims to introduce new voter ID requirements. Weber has opposed that measure. Wagner has also pushed for faster results during the ballot counting process.
Insurance commissioner
Democrats Jane Kim, a former San Francisco supervisor, and state Sen. Ben Allen are competing to become California's next insurance commissioner. The office is responsible for regulating the state's insurance industry, enforcing insurance laws and addressing consumer complaints.
The next commissioner will take office as California continues to grapple with rising insurance costs, wildfire-related losses and insurers limiting or withdrawing coverage in parts of the state.
The candidates have offered different approaches to addressing the insurance market, including questions about affordability, consumer protections and the availability of coverage.
Insurance Commissioner Ricardo Lara was unable to run for re-election due to term limits.
Superintendent of Public Instruction
Richard Barrera and Sonja Shaw are competing to become California's next superintendent of public instruction, succeeding Tony Thurmond, who reached his term limit.
The superintendent is the state's elected chief public school officer and leads the California Department of Education. The office oversees the implementation of state education policies and works with school districts and other education agencies.
Barrera is board president of the San Diego Unified School District, the nation's second-largest district, and has been endorsed by Thurmond. Shaw is a Chino Valley school board president who has been endorsed by Hilton and the Republican Party.
Shaw has vowed to cut bureaucratic waste, demand fiscal transparency and protect fairness in sports for girls. Her district was previously sued by California for adopting a gender notification policy.
Barrerra has touted his district's gains in graduation rates and various academic levels and said he looks forward to improving similar advancements across the state, if elected.
The position is nonpartisan, meaning candidates do not run under party labels on the ballot.
Board of Equalization
California voters will elect members of the State Board of Equalization, which oversees certain tax programs and provides property tax oversight and assistance to county assessors. It is the only board of its kind in the nation.
The board has four elected district members, and voters will choose a candidate for the district in which they live. The candidates on an individual ballot will depend on the voter's location.
Proposition 1: Authorizes $11.25 billion in bonds for housing affordability programs
Proposition 1 would authorize the state to borrow $11.25 billion for housing programs, including affordable rental housing, supportive housing, homeownership and down-payment assistance, veterans' home loans, and housing for farmworkers, tribal communities and students.
The proposal includes funding to build and rehabilitate rental housing and preserve existing affordable units.
A yes vote would allow the state to issue the bonds. A no vote would prevent the borrowing.
The state is expected to pay between $500 million and $600 million annually for about 25 years to repay the bonds.
Proposition 2: Increases California's rainy day fund
Proposition 2 would change the rules around California's state budget reserves and payments toward certain debts, increasing the amount held in the state's rainy day fund.
The reserve fund is intended to help the state maintain essential services during economic downturns, when tax revenues may fall.
A yes vote would change how the state saves money and pays down debt, resulting in higher reserves and requiring additional debt payments for a longer period. A no vote would leave the existing rules in place.
Supporters, including Newsom and Becerra, say the measure would better protect funding for education, healthcare and public safety during economic downturns. No formal opposition was submitted against the measure, though some critics argue that it could limit taxpayer rebates and weaken the effect of the state's constitutional spending limit.
Proposition 3: Makes a high-income tax increase permanent to fund schools and healthcare
Proposition 3 would make permanent an existing increase in state income tax rates for high-income earners. The tax applies to individuals earning more than a threshold initially set at $371,000 and adjusted annually for inflation.
The existing tax increase is set to expire in 2031. If approved, Proposition 3 would extend it indefinitely, maintaining an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion in annual state income tax revenue.
A yes vote would make the tax increase permanent. A no vote would allow it to expire in 2031 under current law.
Supporters including the California Teachers Association and California State PTA say the measure would protect funding for schools and healthcare. Opponents, which include the California Taxpayers Association and California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce, argue that making the tax permanent would increase the long-term tax burden and that the state should address spending concerns first.
Proposition 4: Allows public financing of election campaigns
Proposition 4 would repeal California's ban on state and local governments providing public funding for political campaigns.
If approved, local governments could create their own public campaign financing programs, subject to restrictions on the use of public money. Funds earmarked for education, transportation and public safety could not be used for those programs.
A yes vote would allow state and local governments to create qualifying public financing programs. A no vote would leave the existing ban in place.
Supporters including the League of Women Voters of California and the California Nurses Association say the measure could limit the power and influence of private funding in elections. Opponents, which include the California Taxpayers Association and the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, argue that public money should not be used to finance political campaigns.
Proposition 5: Changes the process for filling vacancies after statewide recall elections
Proposition 5 would change how California fills vacancies when voters recall a statewide elected official.
Under the current system, voters decide whether to remove an official and select a replacement in the same election. The measure would separate those decisions, generally providing for a subsequent special election or an appointment.
A yes vote would remove the replacement candidate question from recall elections. A no vote would preserve the current process.
Supporters say the change would prevent a replacement from winning with only a small share of the vote and could reduce the political and administrative costs of recall elections. Opponents argue that it would take the decision away from voters at the time of a recall and could leave offices vacant while a replacement is selected.
Proposition 37: Creates a loan program for middle-income homebuyers
Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund a state homebuying assistance program for eligible middle-income Californians purchasing newly built homes.
The program would provide fixed-rate loans covering up to 17% of a qualifying home's purchase price. Eligible buyers would have to meet income requirements, occupy the home as their residence and make a down payment of at least 3%.
A yes vote would establish the program and authorize the bonds. A no vote would prevent the state from being required to create it.
The measure's proponents say it would make homeownership more accessible without directly relying on taxpayer-funded bond repayments. The bonds would be repaid through borrowers' mortgage payments.
No formal opposition argument was submitted against the measure, though at least one critic, the League of Women Voters, has said Proposition 37 would fail to confront racial barriers to wealth-building and lower overall costs for families.
Proposition 38: Authorizes bonds for immunology medical research
Proposition 38 would authorize $8.4 billion in state bonds to fund research into immunology and immunotherapy, including efforts to prevent and treat diseases.

PROP
43
LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT SERVICES. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Limits voters’ ability to pass voter-proposed local special taxes by increasing percentage of votes needed to approve such ballot measures from a majority (over 50%) to two-thirds, beginning January 1, 2027. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that local government tax revenues will not go up as much in the future due to a higher vote threshold for certain taxes. Supporters: California Taxpayers Association; Family Business Association of California; California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce Opponents: California Professional Firefighters; California Federation of Teachers; Nurse Alliance of SEIU CA.
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Prop. 43 protects taxpayers by restoring Proposition 13’s two-thirds vote requirement to pass local special taxes, including sales taxes, real estate taxes and utility taxes. Courts have allowed special interests to pass earmarked tax increases with fewer votes. Prop. 43 closes this loophole, protecting taxpayers, homeowners and renters. Vote yes.
CON
PROPOSITION 43 LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO FUND ESSENTIAL LOCAL SERVICES including fire protection, 911 response, schools, roads, hospitals and affordable housing. It doesn’t cut your taxes and lets just 33.4% of voters veto what nearly 67% want. Protect your vote and majority rule. Vote NO on Proposition 43.

# Proposition 43: Limits Voters' Ability to Raise Revenues For Local Government Services
## Proposition 43: Limits Voters' Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
### Additional Titles
Two-Thirds Vote Requirement for Local Special Tax Initiatives and Property Tax Initiative Prohibition Amendment
### Summary
Placed on the ballot via 2025-2026 Assembly Constitutional Amendment 22 (ACA 22), Proposition 43 proposes adding Section 4.5 to Article XII of the California Constitution.
The measure increases the approval threshold for citizen-initiated local special tax measures, requiring a two-thirds (66.67%) vote to enact, extend, or raise special taxes at the local level.
### F iscal Impact
There is a possibility that local government tax revenues will not go up as much in the future due to a higher vote threshold for certain taxes.
### What your vote means
YES: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
NO: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.

# Proposition 43
## Analysis of Measure
### Proposal
***Requires Certain Local Taxes Receive Two-Thirds Approval by Voters.*** Under current law, local taxes that are used for a specific purpose require a two-thirds vote to be approved.
These are called special taxes.
However, recent court decisions have allowed special taxes that are *proposed by voters* to be approved with a majority vote.
Under Proposition 43, beginning on January 1, 2027, any new, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters would require a two-thirds vote.
### Fiscal Effects
As a result, local governments’ tax revenues could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be.
The actual revenue impact is unknown and would depend on future decisions by local governments and voters.
## Yes/No Statement
A **YES** vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
A **NO** vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . Forty-two percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the percentage of voters needed to approve local special taxes from a majority to two-thirds; 55 percent would vote no. How this is built
Proposition 43 is forecast as a higher bars to pass measure whose Yes vote leans Republican . Comparable measures from 2018 to 2024 set how far its Yes share moves with California 's partisanship, and each county moves with its own age, education, race and density mix as well as its 2024 presidential vote, so no two counties share a margin by default. How it reached the ballot moves it further. Proposition 43: Limits Voters' Ability to Raise Revenues For Local Government Services
Proposition 43: Limits Voters' Ability to Raise Revenues For Local Government Services
Proposition 43: Limits Voters' Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
Two-Thirds Vote Requirement for Local Special Tax Initiatives and Property Tax Initiative Prohibition Amendment
Summary
Placed on the ballot via 2025-2026 Assembly Constitutional Amendment 22 (ACA 22 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22) ), Proposition 43 proposes adding Section 4.5 to Article XII of the California Constitution. The measure increases the approval threshold for citizen-initiated local special tax measures, requiring a two-thirds (66.67%) vote to enact, extend, or raise special taxes at the local level.
F iscal Impact
There is a possibility that local government tax revenues will not go up as much in the future due to a higher vote threshold for certain taxes.
What your vote means
YES: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
NO: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters argue that Proposition 43 protects taxpayers by requiring a two-thirds voter majority for local special tax increases, closing legal loopholes that previously allowed them to pass with a simple majority.
Opponents contend that this higher voting threshold allows a minority of voters to block popular measures, making it much harder for local communities to fund essential public services like schools, roads, and emergency response. Ultimately, the measure pits stronger taxpayer protections against the ability of local communities to raise funding by majority rule.
